title: Nitzavim: choose life (Deuteronomy 30:19)
hookLine: "I have set before thee life and death... therefore choose life"

lines: THE SAME WORD IN THE TORAH.
cards: At Jewish celebrations, sooner or later someone lifts a glass and says l'chaim. To life. Over wine at a wedding, over whiskey at a bris, over a paper cup at a retirement party.

It's so ordinary that it's easy to miss what the toast picks: not luck, not health, not money. Life. Today's verse puts that same word, chayim, life, at the center of the choice Moses sets before the people.

teach.h: LIFE AND DEATH, SET BEFORE YOU.
teach.b: Moses is near the end of his speech. He calls heaven and earth to witness and says: "I have set before thee life and death, the blessing and the curse; therefore choose life, that thou mayest live, thou and thy seed."
Notice the odd extra step. If someone offered you life or death, you wouldn't need advice about which to pick. So why say it?
Rashi imagines a father with his son. He stands the boy in front of the best plot of his land and says: choose this one for yourself. The advice isn't there because the answer is hard to see.

Another reading hears the verse as a statement that the choice is real. Maimonides, the philosopher and legal scholar, drew on this chapter in his teaching on free will. A person isn't fated to be good or bad.
And the verses right after say what life means here: to love God, to listen, to hold fast. Life, in this verse, is more than breathing. It's a way of living that leads to more life.
Then the last words: thou and thy seed. Your choice reaches your children. Choosing life is rarely one big moment.
It's made of small ones: a glass lifted, a meal shared, a hard thing faced instead of avoided, a day lived toward something good.

how: 'Choose life' is often quoted in Jewish teaching on ethics and free will, and the toast l'chaim, 'to life', is a familiar sound at Jewish celebrations.

o: standing, the people gathered before Moses
chosen, the people picked out by God
listening, the people hearing the law read

games.q: inside choose life — tap the pairs.
p: a father pointing to the best plot
free will: the choice is real

s: since the right choice is obvious, the verse gives no advice
it adds advice anyway: therefore choose life.
Maimonides drew on this chapter in his teaching on free will
a person isn't fated; each can choose.

games.q: a father shows his son the best field he owns, and the worst. in Rashi's picture, what does the father do?
o: lets the son guess, to test him.
says: choose this good one for yourself.
chooses for him without a word.
games.why: the choice stays the son's, but the father points. that's how Rashi hears 'therefore choose life'.

practice: Think about the rest of today and find one fork in it, maybe a small one: eat something real or skip it, go outside or stay in, call someone or keep scrolling, rest or push through when you shouldn't.
Name it, and picture taking the side that gives a little more life, to you or to someone else.

wordCard.voice: Nitzavim. Standing. And the choice set before everyone standing there: life.

carryVoice: Your line: choose life. And if you lift a glass tonight, you'll know the toast. Day five hundred twenty-one, done.
